contenido: 1. At the beginning of the new millennium, as the Great Jubilee in which we celebrated the two thousand years of the birth of Jesus closes and a new stage of its journey opens for the Church, the words with which one day Jesus, after having spoken to the crowd from Simon's boat, invited the Apostle to "row out into the deep" to fish resonate in our hearts: "Duc in altum" (Lc 5,4). Peter and the first companions trusted the word of Christ and let down their nets. «And when they had done so, they gathered an enormous quantity of fish» (Lc 5,6).

2. Therefore, I feel the duty to address all of you to share the song of praise. I had thought of this Holy Year of two thousand as an important moment since the beginning of my Pontificate. I thought of this celebration as a providential call in which the Church, thirty-five years after the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, would have been invited to question its renewal to assume its evangelizing mission with new impetus.

3. Above all, dear brothers and sisters, it is necessary to think about the future that awaits us. So many times during these months, we have looked towards the new millennium that is opening, living the Jubilee not only as a memory of the past, but as a prophecy of the future. It is now necessary to take advantage of the treasure of grace received, translating it into fervent purposes and concrete lines of action. It is a task to which I wish to invite all local Churches. In each of them, gathered around the Bishop himself, in listening to the Word, in fraternal communion and in the "breaking of bread" (cf. Hch 2,42), the Church of Christ, one, holy, catholic and apostolic, is "truly present and active"[1]. It is especially in the concrete reality of each Church where the mystery of the one People of God assumes that special configuration that makes it suitable for all contexts and cultures.

4. «We thank you, Lord, almighty God» (Ap 11,17). In the Bull calling for the Jubilee, he predicted that the bimillennial celebration of the mystery of the Incarnation would be lived as a “single and uninterrupted song of praise to the Trinity”[2] and at the same time as a path of reconciliation and as a sign of genuine hope for those who look to Christ and his Church”[3]. The experience of the Jubilee Year has moved precisely in these vital dimensions, reaching moments of intensity that have made us feel like touching with our hands the merciful presence of God, from whom comes "every good gift and every perfect gift" (St 1,17).

5. The coincidence of this Jubilee with the entry into a new millennium has certainly favored, without giving in to millenarian fantasies, the perception of the mystery of Christ in the great horizon of the history of salvation. Christianity is the religion that has entered history! Indeed, it is on the terrain of history where God wanted to establish an alliance with Israel and thus prepare the birth of the Son from the womb of Mary, "in the fullness of time" (Ga 4,4). Contemplated in his divine and human mystery, Christ is the foundation and center of history, of which he is the meaning and ultimate goal. In fact, it is through him, the Word and image of the Father, that "everything was made" (Jn 1,3; cf. Col 1,15). His incarnation, culminated in the paschal mystery and in the gift of the Spirit, is the axis of time, the mysterious hour in which the Kingdom of God has become close (cf. Mc 1,15), moreover, it has placed its roots, like a seed destined to become a great tree (cf. Mc 4,30-32), in our history.

6. So that we could contemplate the mystery with a purer gaze, this Jubilee Year has been strongly characterized by the request for forgiveness. And this has been true not only for each one individually, who has examined his own life to implore mercy and obtain the special gift of indulgence, but also for the entire Church, which has wanted to remember the infidelities with which so many of her children, throughout history, have darkened her face as the Bride of Christ.

7. However, the lively penitential conscience has not prevented us from giving glory to the Lord for all that he has done throughout the centuries, and especially in the century that we have left behind, granting his Church a great multitude of saints and martyrs. For some of them the Jubilee Year has also been the year of their beatification or canonization. With respect to well-known Pontiffs in history or humble lay and religious figures, from one continent to another in the world, holiness has manifested itself more than ever as the dimension that best expresses the mystery of the Church. Eloquent message that does not need words, holiness represents the face of Christ vividly.

8. Following in the footsteps of the Saints, countless children of the Church have come here to Rome, before the tombs of the Apostles, eager to profess their own faith, confess their own sins and receive the mercy that saves. My gaze this year has been impressed not only by the crowds that have filled St. Peter's Square during many celebrations. I have frequently stopped to look at the long lines of pilgrims patiently waiting to cross the Holy Door. In each one of them he tried to imagine the story of his life, full of joys, anxieties and pains; a story of encounter with Christ and that in dialogue with him he resumed his path of hope.

9. The numerous jubilee meetings have brought together the most diverse classes of people, with truly impressive participation noted, which has sometimes tested the efforts of the organizers and animators, both ecclesial and civil. I wish to take advantage of this Letter to express my most cordial gratitude to all of them. But, in addition to the number, what has moved me so many times has been to confirm the serious effort of prayer, reflection and communion that these meetings have manifested.

10. Obviously I cannot go into details about all the jubilee celebrations. Each of them has had its characteristics and has left its message not only to those who have attended directly, but also to those who have known it or have participated remotely through social media. But how can we not remember the festive tone of the first major meeting dedicated to children? Starting with them meant, in a way, respecting Jesus' exhortation: "Let the children come to me" (Mc 10,14). Furthermore, perhaps it meant repeating the gesture he made when he "placed a child in the middle" and presented him as the very symbol of the attitude that had to be assumed if one wanted to enter the Kingdom of God (cf. Mt 18,2-4).

11. In the logic of this Jubilee Year, the International Eucharistic Congress should have a determining meaning. And he had it! If the Eucharist is the sacrifice of Christ who makes himself present among us, how could his real presence not be the center of the Holy Year dedicated to the incarnation of the Word? Precisely for this reason it was planned as an "intensely Eucharistic" year[6] and that is how we have tried to live it. At the same time, how could the memory of the Mother be missing, next to the memory of the birth of the Son? Mary has been present in the jubilee celebrations not only through timely and qualified congresses, but above all through the great Act of consecration with which, surrounded by a good part of the world Episcopate, I entrusted to her maternal care the lives of the men and women of the new millennium.

12. It will thus be understood that he speaks spontaneously of the Jubilee seen from the See of Peter. However, I do not forget that I myself wanted its celebration to take place in full right also in the particular Churches, and it is there that the majority of the faithful have been able to obtain the special graces and, in particular, the indulgence of the Jubilee Year. Therefore, it is significant that many Dioceses have felt the desire to be present, with numerous groups of faithful, also here in Rome. The Eternal City has, therefore, once again manifested its providential role as a place where the riches and gifts of each and every one of the Churches, and also of each nation and culture, are harmonized in "catholicity", so that the one Church of Christ manifests in an increasingly eloquent way its mystery of sacrament of unity.[7]

13. How can I not also remember my personal Jubilee on the roads of the Holy Land? I would have liked to begin it in Ur of the Chaldeans, to practically follow in the footsteps of Abraham "our father in faith" (cf. Rm 4,11-16). Instead, I had to content myself with a purely spiritual stage, through the suggestive "Liturgy of the Word" celebrated on February 23 in the Paul VI Hall. Then the true pilgrimage took place, following the itinerary of salvation history. Thus I had the joy of standing on Mount Sinai, a place that remembers the delivery of the Decalogue and the first Covenant. A month later I returned to the path, reaching Mount Nebo and then visiting the same places inhabited and sanctified by the Redeemer. It is difficult to express the emotion I experienced when being able to venerate the places of Christ's birth and life, in Bethlehem and Nazareth, when celebrating the Eucharist in the Cenacle, in the same place of his institution, when meditating on the mystery of the Cross on Golgotha, where he gave his life for us. In those places, still so tested and even recently saddened by violence, I was able to experience an extraordinary welcome not only from the children of the Church, but also from the Israeli and Palestinian communities. Great was my emotion in the prayer before the Wailing Wall and during the visit to the Yad Vashem Mausoleum, in the terrifying memory of the victims of the Nazi extermination camps. That pilgrimage was a moment of brotherhood and peace, which I am pleased to point out as one of the most beautiful gifts of the jubilee event. Thinking about the climate experienced in those days, I express the sincere wish for a prompt and just solution to the problems still open in those holy places, so dear to the Jews, Christians and Muslims at the same time.

14. The Jubilee has also been, and it could not be otherwise, a great event of charity. From the preparatory years, I called for greater and more committed attention to the problems of poverty that still afflict the world. In this regard, the problem of the international debt of poor countries has had a particular significance. In relation to these, a gesture of generosity was in the very logic of the Jubilee, which in its original biblical configuration was precisely the time in which the community committed itself to reestablish justice and solidarity in relationships between people, also restoring stolen material goods. I am pleased to note that recently the Parliaments of many creditor States have voted for a substantial reduction in the bilateral debt owed by the poorest and most indebted Countries. I express my wishes so that the respective Governments comply, in a short period of time, with these parliamentary decisions. More problematic, however, has been the issue of multilateral debt, contracted by poor countries with international financial organizations. It is to be hoped that the member states of such organizations, especially those that have greater influence in the decisions, will be able to find the necessary consensus to reach a quick solution to an issue on which the development process of many countries depends, with serious consequences for the economic and existential condition of so many people.

15. These are some of the most outstanding aspects of the jubilee experience. This one leaves us with so many memories. But if we wanted to identify the essential core of the great heritage that he leaves us, I would not hesitate to concretize it in the contemplation of the face of Christ: contemplated in its historical coordinates and in its mystery, welcomed in his multiple presence in the Church and in the world, confessed as the meaning of history and the light of our path.

16. « We want to see Jesus » (Jn 12,21). This request, made to the Apostle Philip by some Greeks who had come to Jerusalem for the Easter pilgrimage, has also resonated spiritually in our ears in this Jubilee Year. Like those pilgrims of two thousand years ago, the men of our time, perhaps not always consciously, ask today's believers not only to "speak" about Christ, but in a certain way to make him "see." And perhaps it is not the Church's task to reflect the light of Christ in each era of history and also to make his face shine before the generations of the new millennium?

17. The contemplation of the face of Christ focuses above all on what the Holy Scripture says about him, which, from beginning to end, is impregnated with this mystery, obscurely indicated in the Old Testament and fully revealed in the New, to the point that Saint Jerome vigorously affirms: "To ignore the Scriptures is to ignore Christ himself"[8]. Having Scripture as a foundation, we open ourselves to the action of the Spirit (cf. Jn 15,26), which is the origin of those writings, and, at the same time, to the testimony of the Apostles (cf. ibíd., 27), who had the living experience of Christ, the Word of life, saw him with their eyes, heard him with their ears and touched him with their hands (cf. 1 Jn 1,1).

18. In reality the Gospels do not claim to be a complete biography of Jesus according to the canons of modern historical science. However, the face of the Nazarene emerges from them with a secure historical foundation, since the evangelists took care to present it by collecting reliable testimonies (cf. Lc 1,3) and working on documents submitted to attentive ecclesiastical discernment. On the basis of these initial testimonies they, under the enlightened action of the Holy Spirit, discovered the humanly disconcerting fact of the virgin birth of Jesus to Mary, wife of Joseph. From those who had known him during the almost thirty years he spent in Nazareth (cf. Lc 3,23), they collected information about his life as a "carpenter's son" (Mt 13,55) and also as a "carpenter", among his relatives (cf. Mc 6,3). They talked about his religiosity, which moved him to go with his family on an annual pilgrimage to the temple of Jerusalem (cf. Lc 2,41) and especially because he regularly went to the synagogue in his city (cf. Lc 4,16).

19. «The disciples were glad to see the Lord» (Jn 20,20). The face that the Apostles beheld after the resurrection was the same as that of Jesus with whom they had lived for about three years, and who now convinced them of the astonishing truth of his new life by showing them "his hands and his side" (ibíd.). It certainly wasn't easy to believe. The disciples of Emmaus believed only after a laborious journey of the spirit (cf. Lc 24,13-35). The apostle Thomas believed only after having verified the prodigy (cf. Jn 20,24-29). In reality, even if one saw and touched his body, only faith could unlock the mystery of that face. This was an experience that the disciples must have already had in the historical life of Christ, with the questions that arose in their minds every time they felt challenged by his gestures and words. Jesus is only truly reached by faith, through a path whose stages the Gospel presents to us in the well-known scene of Caesarea Philippi (cf. Mt 16,13-20). To the disciples, as if making a first assessment of his mission, Jesus asks who the "people" say he is, receiving the answer: "Some, John the Baptist; others, that Elijah; others, that Jeremiah or one of the prophets » (Mt 16,14). High response, but still distant – and how much! – from the truth. The people get a glimpse of the truly exceptional religious dimension of this rabbi who speaks in a fascinating way, but fails to place him among the men of God who marked the history of Israel. In reality, Jesus is very different! It is precisely this further degree of knowledge, which concerns the deep level of his person, what he expects from "his own": "And you, who do you say that I am?" » (Mt 16,15). Only the faith professed by Peter, and with him by the Church of all times, truly reaches the heart, going to the depth of the mystery: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mt 16,16).

20. How did Peter come to this faith? And what is asked of us if we want to follow in his footsteps with ever more conviction? Matthew gives us a clarifying indication in the words with which Jesus welcomes Peter's confession: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven" (16,17). The expression "flesh and blood" evokes man and the common way of knowing. This, in the case of Jesus, is not enough. A grace of "revelation" that comes from the Father is necessary (cf. ibíd.). Luke offers us information that follows the same direction, noting that this dialogue with the disciples took place while Jesus "was praying alone" (Lc 9,18). Both indications make us aware of the fact that we do not arrive at full contemplation of the face of the Lord with our strength alone, but by allowing ourselves to be guided by grace. Only the experience of silence and prayer offers the adequate horizon in which the most authentic, faithful and coherent knowledge of that mystery can mature and develop, which has its culminating expression in the solemn proclamation of the evangelist John: "And the Word became flesh, and made his Dwelling among us, and we have contemplated his glory, glory that he receives from the Father as the only Son, full of grace and truth" (Jn 1,14).

21. The Word and the flesh, the divine glory and its dwelling among men! In the intimate and inseparable union of these two polarities is the identity of Christ, according to the classic formulation of the Council of Chalcedon (a. 451): "One person in two natures." The person is that, and only that, the eternal Word, the son of the Father. His two natures, without any confusion, but without any possible separation, are the divine and the human[10].

22. «The Word became flesh» (Jn 1,14). This splendid Johannine presentation of the mystery of Christ is confirmed throughout the New Testament. The apostle Paul also places himself in this sense when he affirms that the Son of God was born of the line of David "according to the flesh" (Rm 1,3; cf. 9,5). If today, with the rationalism that reigns in much of contemporary culture, it is above all the faith in the divinity of Christ that constitutes a problem, in other historical and cultural contexts there was rather a tendency to downgrade or ignore the concrete historical aspect of the humanity of Jesus. But for the faith of the Church it is essential and inalienable to affirm that the Word really "became flesh" and assumed all the characteristics of the human being, except sin (cf. Hb 4,15). In this perspective, the Incarnation is truly a kenosis, a "putting off," on the part of the Son of God, of the glory that he has had from eternity (cf. Flp 2,6-8; 1 P 3,18).

23. «Lord, I seek your face» (Sal 2726,8). The ancient longing of the Psalmist could not receive a better and surprising answer than in the contemplation of the face of Christ. In him God has truly blessed us and made “his face shine on us” (Sal 6766,3). At the same time, God and man as he is, Christ also reveals to us the authentic face of man, "fully manifesting man to man himself"[11].

24. This divine-human identity springs vigorously from the Gospels, which offer us a series of elements thanks to which we can enter the "limit zone" of the mystery, represented by the self-consciousness of Christ. The Church does not doubt that in their narrative the evangelists, inspired by the Holy Spirit, correctly captured, in the words spoken by Jesus, the truth that he had about his conscience and his person. Isn't this perhaps what Luke wants to tell us, recording the first words of Jesus, barely twelve years old, in the temple of Jerusalem? Then he appears already conscious of having a unique relationship with God, such as that of the "son." In fact, to his Mother, who points out the anguish with which she and Joseph have searched for him, Jesus responds without hesitation: "Why were you looking for me?" Did you not know that I should be in my Father's house? » (Lc 2,49). It is not surprising, then, that, in maturity, his language firmly expressed the depth of his mystery, as is abundantly emphasized both by the Synoptic Gospels (cf. Mt 11,27; Lc 10,22), and by the evangelist John. In his self-awareness Jesus has no doubts: «The Father is in me, and I in the Father» (Jn 10,38).

25. Contemplation of the face of Christ thus leads us to approach the most paradoxical aspect of his mystery, as seen in the extreme hour, the hour of the Cross. Mystery in the mystery, before which the human being must prostrate himself in adoration.

26. The cry of Jesus on the cross, dear brothers and sisters, does not reveal the anguish of a desperate person, but rather the prayer of the Son who offers his life to the Father in love for the salvation of all. While he identifies himself with our sin, "abandoned" by the Father, he "abandons" himself in the hands of the Father. Fix your eyes on the Father. Precisely because of the knowledge and experience that only he has of God, even in this moment of darkness he clearly sees the gravity of sin and suffers for it. Only he, who sees the Father and enjoys him fully, deeply values ​​what it means to resist his love with sin. Even before, and much more than in the body, his passion is atrocious suffering of the soul. The theological tradition has not avoided asking how Jesus could experience at the same time the profound union with the Father, a natural source of joy and happiness, and the agony up to the cry of abandonment. The copresence of these two seemingly irreconcilable dimensions is actually rooted in the unfathomable depth of the hypostatic union.

27. Faced with this mystery, in addition to theological research, we can find effective help in that heritage that is the "lived theology" of the Saints. They offer us precious indications that allow us to more easily welcome the intuition of faith, and this thanks to the particular lights that some of them have received from the Holy Spirit, or even through the experience that they themselves have made of the terrible states of trial that mystical tradition describes as "dark night." Many times the Saints have lived something similar to the experience of Jesus on the cross in the paradoxical confluence of happiness and pain. In the Dialogue of Divine Providence, God the Father shows Catherine of Siena how joy can be present along with suffering in holy souls: «And the soul is happy and suffering: sorrowful for the sins of its neighbor, happy for the union and for the affection of the charity that it has received in itself. They imitate the immaculate Lamb, my Only Begotten Son, who, being on the cross, was happy and suffering »[13]. In the same way, Therese of Lisieux lives her agony in communion with that of Jesus, verifying in herself precisely the same paradox of Jesus happy and anguished: «Our Lord in the Garden of Olives enjoyed all the joys of the Trinity, however his agony was no less cruel. It is a mystery, but I assure you that, from what I try myself, I understand something »[14]. It is a very clear testimony. On the other hand, the same narrative of the evangelists gives rise to this ecclesiastical perception of the consciousness of Christ when it remembers that, even in his deep pain, he dies imploring forgiveness for his executioners (cf. Lc 23,34) and expressing to the Father his extreme filial abandonment: "Father, in your hands I put my spirit" (Lc 23,46).

28. As on Friday and Holy Saturday, the Church remains in contemplation of this bloody face, in which the life of God is hidden and the salvation of the world is offered. But this contemplation of the face of Christ cannot be reduced to his crucified image. He is the Risen One! If it were not so, our preaching would be vain and our faith would be vain (cf. 1 Co 15,14). The resurrection was the Father's response to the obedience of Christ, as the Letter to the Hebrews recalls: "Who, having offered prayers and supplications in the days of his mortal life with powerful cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, was heard for his reverent attitude, and even though he was a Son, he experienced obedience with what he suffered; and having become perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him" (5,7-9).

29. «Behold, I am with you always until the end of the world» (Mt 28,20). This certainty, dear brothers and sisters, has accompanied the Church for two millennia and has now been revived in our hearts by the celebration of the Jubilee. From it we must draw renewed impetus in the Christian life, also making it the inspiring force of our path. Aware of this presence of the Risen Lord among us, today we ask ourselves the question addressed to Peter in Jerusalem, immediately after his Pentecost speech: «What are we to do, brothers? » (Hch 2,37).

30. First of all, I do not hesitate to say that the perspective in which the pastoral path must be placed is that of holiness. Was this not the ultimate meaning of the Jubilee indulgence, as a special grace offered by Christ so that the life of each baptized person could be deeply purified and renewed?

31. Remembering this elementary truth, placing it as the foundation of the pastoral programming that binds us at the beginning of the new millennium, might seem, at first, something impractical. Can holiness be "programmed"? What can this word mean in the logic of a pastoral plan?

32. For this pedagogy of holiness, a Christianity that distinguishes itself above all in the art of prayer is necessary. The Jubilee Year has been a year of more intense personal and community prayer. But we know well that praying is not something that can be taken for granted either. It is necessary to learn to pray, as if learning this art again from the very lips of the divine Master, like the first disciples: "Lord, teach us to pray" (Lc 11,1). In prayer, that dialogue with Christ develops that makes us his intimates: "Remain in me, as I remain in you" (Jn 15,4). This reciprocity is the very foundation, the soul of the Christian life and a condition for all authentic pastoral life. Realized in us by the Holy Spirit, it opens us, through Christ and in Christ, to the contemplation of the face of the Father. Learning this Trinitarian logic of Christian prayer, living it fully first of all in the liturgy, the summit and source of ecclesial life[17], but also from personal experience, is the secret of a truly vital Christianity, which has no reason to fear the future, because it continually returns to the sources and is regenerated in them.

33. Is it not a "sign of the times" that today, despite the vast processes of secularization, a diffuse demand for spirituality is detected, which is largely manifested precisely in a renewed need to pray? Other religions, already widely present in the territories of ancient Christianity, also offer their own responses to this need, and sometimes do so in an attractive way. We, who have the grace to believe in Christ, revealer of the Father and Savior of the world, must teach us to what degree of interiorization our relationship with him can lead us.

34. Certainly, the faithful who have received the gift of the vocation to a life of special consecration are called in a particular way to prayer: by its nature, consecration makes them more available for the contemplative experience, and it is important that they cultivate it with generous dedication. But anyone who thinks that ordinary Christians can settle for superficial prayer, incapable of filling their lives, is mistaken. Especially in the face of so many ways in which today's world tests faith, they would not only be mediocre Christians, but "Christians at risk." Indeed, they would run the insidious risk of their faith progressively weakening, and perhaps they would end up giving in to the seduction of substitutes, embracing alternative religious proposals and even compromising with extravagant forms of superstition. It is necessary, therefore, that education in prayer become in some way a determining point of all pastoral programming. I myself have proposed to dedicate the next Wednesday catechesis to reflection on the Psalms, beginning with those of the Lauds prayer, with which the Church invites us to "consecrate" and guide our day. How much it would help if, not only in religious communities, but also in parish communities, we made more efforts so that the entire spiritual environment was marked by prayer. It would be advisable to value, with appropriate discernment, the popular forms and above all to educate in the liturgical ones. The day is perhaps closer than is commonly believed when, in the Christian community, the multiple pastoral commitments and witness in the world are combined with the Eucharistic celebration and perhaps with the prayer of Lauds and Vespers. This is demonstrated by the experience of so many groups committed to Christianity, even with a good representation of lay people.

35. The greatest effort must therefore be placed on the liturgy, "the summit towards which the activity of the Church tends and at the same time the source from which all its strength flows"[19]. In the 20th century, especially since the Council, the Christian community has gained a lot in the way of celebrating the Sacraments and especially the Eucharist. It is necessary to insist on this sense, giving particular emphasis to the Sunday Eucharist and to Sunday itself, felt as a special day of faith, day of the risen Lord and the gift of the Spirit, true Easter of the week[20]. For two thousand years, Christian time has been marked by the memory of that "first day after the Sabbath" (Mc 16,2.9; Lc 24,1; Jn 20,1¿, en el que Cristo resucitado llevó a los Apóstoles el don de la paz y del Espíritu (cf. Jn 20,19-23). The truth of the resurrection of Christ is the original data on which the Christian faith is based (cf. 1 Co 15,14), an event that is the center of the mystery of time and that prefigures the last day, when Christ returns in glory. We do not know what events the millennium that is beginning will hold for us, but we are certain that it will remain firmly in the hands of Christ, the "King of Kings and Lord of Lords" (Ap 19,16) and precisely by celebrating his Easter, not only once a year but every Sunday, the Church will continue to indicate to each generation "what constitutes the central axis of history, with which the mystery of the beginning and the final destiny of the world are related"[21].

contenido: 36. Therefore, I would like to insist, in line with the Exhortation "Dies Domini", that participation in the Eucharist be, for each baptized person, the center of Sunday. It is an inalienable duty, which must be lived not only to fulfill a precept, but as a necessity for a truly conscious and coherent Christian life. We are entering a millennium that is characterized by a deep network of cultures and religions even in countries of ancient Christianization. In many regions Christians are, or are being, a "little flock" (Lc 12,32). This challenges them to bear witness more strongly, often in conditions of loneliness and difficulty, to the specific aspects of their own identity. The duty of Eucharistic participation every Sunday is one of these. The Sunday Eucharist, gathering Christians weekly as the family of God around the table of the Word and the Bread of life, is also the most natural antidote against dispersion. It is the privileged place where communion is constantly announced and cultivated. Precisely through Eucharistic participation, the Lord's Day also becomes the day of the Church[22], which can thus effectively play its role as a sacrament of unity.

37. I would also like to ask for renewed pastoral courage so that the daily pedagogy of the Christian community knows how to propose in a convincing and effective way the practice of the Sacrament of Reconciliation. As you will remember, in 1984 I intervened on this topic with the post-synodal Exhortation Reconciliatio et paenitentia, which collected the fruits of the reflection of an Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, dedicated to this problem. Then he invited us to make every effort to confront the crisis of the "sense of sin" that occurs in contemporary culture[23], but even more so, he invited us to discover Christ as mysterium pietatis, in which God shows us his merciful heart and fully reconciles us to himself. This is the face of Christ that should also be revealed through the sacrament of penance which, for a Christian, "is the ordinary way to obtain forgiveness and remission of serious sins committed after Baptism"[24]. When the aforementioned Synod faced the problem, the crisis of the Sacrament was evident to everyone, especially in some regions of the world. The reasons behind it have not faded away in this short period of time. But the Jubilee Year, which has been particularly characterized by the recourse to sacramental Penance, has offered us an encouraging message, which should not be wasted: if many, among them so many young people, have fruitfully approached this sacrament, it is probably necessary for Pastors to have greater confidence, creativity and perseverance in presenting it and valuing it. We must not give up, dear brother priests, in the face of contemporary crises! The gifts of the Lord - and the Sacraments are among the most precious - come from Him who knows well the heart of man and is the Lord of history.

38. In the programming that awaits us, working with greater confidence in a pastoral ministry that gives priority to prayer, personal and community, means respecting an essential principle of the Christian vision of life: the primacy of grace. There is a temptation that always plagues every spiritual path and pastoral action itself: to think that the results depend on our ability to do and program. Certainly, God asks us for real collaboration with his grace and, therefore, invites us to use all the resources of our intelligence and operational capacity in our service to the cause of the Kingdom. But we must not forget that, without Christ, "we can do nothing" (cf. Jn 15,5).

39. There is no doubt that this primacy of holiness and prayer can only be conceived from a renewed listening to the word of God. Since the Second Vatican Council has emphasized the preeminent role of the word of God in the life of the Church, much progress has certainly been made in the assiduous listening and attentive reading of the Holy Scripture. She has received her due honor in the public prayer of the Church. Both individuals and communities already turn to Scripture in large numbers, and among the laity themselves there are many who dedicate themselves to it with the valuable help of theological and biblical studies. Precisely with this attention to the word of God, the task of evangelization and catechesis is mainly being revitalized. It is necessary, dear brothers and sisters, to consolidate and deepen this orientation, including through the dissemination of the Bible in families. It is necessary, in particular, that listening to the Word becomes a vital encounter, in the ancient and always valid tradition of lectio divina, which allows us to find in the biblical text the living word that challenges, guides and models existence.

40. Feeding on the Word to be "servants of the Word" in the commitment to evangelization is undoubtedly a priority for the Church at the beginning of the new millennium. The situation of a "Christian society" has already passed, even in the countries of ancient evangelization, which, even with multiple human weaknesses, was based explicitly on evangelical values. Today we must bravely face a situation that is increasingly varied and compromised, in the context of globalization and the new and changing situation of peoples and cultures that characterizes it. I have repeated many times in these years the "call" to the new evangelization. I reiterate it now, above all to indicate that we need to rekindle in us the impulse of our origins, allowing ourselves to be impregnated by the ardor of apostolic preaching after Pentecost. We must relive in ourselves the compelling feeling of Paul, who exclaimed: "woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel!" » (1 Co 9,16).

41. May the splendid example of so many witnesses of the faith that the Jubilee has reminded us help and guide us in this confident, enterprising and creative missionary action. The Church has always found, in its martyrs, a seed of life. Sanguis martyrum - semen christianorum[25]. This famous "law" enunciated by Tertullian has always been proven true under the test of history. Will it not also be like this for the century and for the millennium that we are beginning? Perhaps we were too accustomed to thinking about martyrs in somewhat distant terms, as if they were a group from the past, linked above all to the first centuries of the Christian era. The Jubilee memory has opened up a surprising panorama for us, showing us our times are particularly rich in witnesses who, in one way or another, have known how to live the Gospel in situations of hostility and persecution, often to the point of giving their own blood as supreme proof. In them the word of God, sown in fertile ground, has borne fruit a hundredfold (cf. Mt 13,8.23). With their example they have shown us and almost "paved" the path of the future. It is up to us, with the grace of God, to follow in his footsteps.

42. "By this everyone will know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another" (Jn 13,35). If we have truly contemplated the face of Christ, dear brothers and sisters, our pastoral programming will be inspired by the “new commandment” that he gave us: “As I have loved you, so you also should love one another” (Jn 13,34).

43. Making the Church the home and school of communion: this is the great challenge that we have before us in the millennium that is beginning, if we want to be faithful to God's plan and also respond to the deep hopes of the world.

44. On this basis, the new century must commit us more than ever to value and develop those areas and instruments that, according to the great guidelines of the Second Vatican Council, serve to ensure and guarantee communion. How can we not think, above all, of the specific services of communion that are the Petrine ministry and, closely related to it, episcopal collegiality? These are realities that have their foundation and consistency in the very plan of Christ for the Church[28], but that precisely for this reason need continuous verification to ensure their authentic evangelical inspiration.

45. Spaces of communion must be cultivated and expanded day by day, at all levels, in the fabric of the life of each Church. In it, communion must be evident in the relationships between Bishops, priests and deacons, between Pastors and the entire People of God, between clergy and religious, between associations and ecclesial movements. To achieve this, the participation bodies provided for by Canon Law, such as the Presbyteral and Pastoral Councils, must be increasingly valued. These, as is known, are not inspired by the criteria of parliamentary democracy, since they act in a consultative and non-deliberative manner[29], however, they do not lose their meaning and importance. In fact, the theology and spirituality of communion advise reciprocal and effective listening between Pastors and faithful, on the one hand keeping them united a priori in everything that is essential and, on the other, encouraging them to come together normally even in matters of opinion towards considered and shared options.

46. This perspective of communion is closely linked to the capacity of the Christian community to welcome all the gifts of the Spirit. The unity of the Church is not uniformity, but organic integration of legitimate diversities. It is the reality of many members united in one body, the one Body of Christ (cf. 1 Co 12,12). It is necessary, therefore, for the Church of the third millennium to encourage all the baptized and confirmed to become aware of their own active responsibility in ecclesial life. Along with the ordained ministry, other ministries, instituted or simply recognized, can flourish for the good of the entire community, attending to its multiple needs: from catechesis to liturgical animation, from the education of young people to the most diverse manifestations of charity.

47. Special attention must also be paid to the pastoral care of the family, which is especially necessary in a historical moment like the present, in which a generalized and radical crisis of this fundamental institution is being observed. In the Christian vision of marriage, the relationship between a man and a woman – a reciprocal and total relationship, unique and indissoluble – responds to God's primitive project, obscured in history by "hardness of heart", but which Christ has come to restore in its original splendor, revealing what God has wanted "from the beginning" (cf. Mt 19,8). In marriage, elevated to the dignity of Sacrament, the "great mystery" of Christ's spousal love for his Church is also expressed (cf. Ef 5,32).

48. And what can we say, furthermore, about the urgency of promoting communion in the delicate area of the ecumenical field? The sad legacy of the past still affects us as we cross the threshold of the new millennium. The jubilee celebration has included some truly prophetic and moving signs, but there is still a long way to go.

49. Starting from intra-ecclesial communion, charity opens by its nature to universal service, projecting us towards the practice of an active and concrete love with each human being. This is an area that decisively characterizes Christian life, ecclesial style and pastoral programming. The century and millennium that are beginning will still have to see, and it is to be hoped that they will see it palpably, to what degree of dedication charity can reach towards the poorest. If we have truly started from the contemplation of Christ, we have to know how to discover it above all in the faces of those with whom he himself wanted to identify himself: "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink; I was a stranger and you welcomed me; naked and you have clothed me, sick and you have visited me, imprisoned and you have come to see me » (Mt 25,35-36). This page is not a simple invitation to charity: it is a page of Christology, which illuminates the mystery of Christ. On this page, the Church proves her fidelity as the Bride of Christ, no less than in the area of ​​orthodoxy.

50. In fact, in our time there are many needs that challenge Christian sensitivity. Our world begins the new millennium loaded with the contradictions of economic, cultural, and technological growth, which offers the lucky few great possibilities, leaving not only millions and millions of people on the margins of progress, but also living in living conditions well below the minimum required for human dignity. How is it possible that, in our time, there are still those who are dying of hunger; who is condemned to illiteracy; who lacks the most basic medical care; Who doesn't have a roof to shelter in?

51. Can we remain on the sidelines in the face of the prospects of an ecological imbalance, which makes vast areas of the planet uninhabitable and hostile to man? Or in the face of the problems of peace, often threatened with the nightmare of catastrophic wars? Or in the face of the vilification of the fundamental human rights of so many people, especially children? There are many urgencies to which the Christian spirit cannot remain insensitive.

52. Obviously all this has to be carried out in a specifically Christian style: it must be above all the laity, by virtue of their own vocation, who are present in these tasks, never giving in to the temptation of reducing Christian communities to social agencies. In particular, the relationship with civil society will have to be configured in such a way that it respects the autonomy and powers of the latter, according to the teachings proposed by the social doctrine of the Church.

53. As a sign of this message of charity and human promotion, which is based on the intimate demands of the Gospel, I wanted the Jubilee Year itself, among the numerous fruits of charity that it has already produced in the course of its development - I am thinking particularly of the help offered to so many poorer brothers to make their participation in the Jubilee possible - also leave a work that is, in some way, the fruit and the seal of Jubilee charity. Indeed, many pilgrims have contributed in different ways with their alms and, along with them, many protagonists of the economic world have also offered generous help, which has served to ensure the convenient realization of the jubilee event. Once the expenses that have had to be faced throughout the year have been covered, any money that may be left over must be used for charitable purposes. Indeed, it is important to exclude from such a significant religious event any appearance of economic speculation. What remains will also serve to repeat on this occasion the experience lived so many other times throughout history since, at the beginning of the Church, the community of Jerusalem offered non-Christians the moving image of a spontaneous exchange of gifts, to the communion of goods, in favor of the poorest (cf. Hch 2,44â45).

54. A new century and a new millennium open in the light of Christ. But not everyone sees this light. We have the wonderful and demanding task of being its "reflection." It is the mysterium lunae so dear to the contemplation of the Fathers, who indicated with this image that the Church depended on Christ, the Sun from which she reflects the light[38]. It was a way of expressing what Christ himself says, when he presented himself as "the light of the world" (Jn 8,12) and at the same time asked his disciples to be "the light of the world" (cf Mt 5,14).

55. In this perspective also lies the great challenge of interreligious dialogue, in which we will still be committed during the new century, in the line indicated by the Second Vatican Council[39]. In the years of preparation for the Great Jubilee, the Church, through meetings of notable symbolic interest, has tried to establish a relationship of openness and dialogue with representatives of other religions. The dialogue must continue. In the situation of a marked cultural and religious pluralism, as it is being presented in the society of the new millennium, this dialogue is also important to propose a firm basis for peace and remove the disastrous specter of religious wars that have bathed so many periods in the history of humanity in blood. The name of the one God must increasingly be, as it already is, a name of peace and an imperative of peace.

56. But dialogue cannot be based on religious indifference, and we as Christians have the duty to develop it by offering full testimony to the hope that is in us (cf. 1 Pt 3,15). We must not fear that what may constitute an offense to the identity of the other is what, on the other hand, is a joyful announcement of a gift for all, and which is proposed to all with the greatest respect for the freedom of each: the gift of the revelation of the God-Love, who "so loved the world that he gave it his only begotten Son" (Jn 3,16). All of this, as has also been recently highlighted by the Dominus Iesus Declaration, cannot be the object of a kind of dialogic negotiation, as if for us it were a simple opinion. On the contrary, for us it is a grace that fills us with joy, news that we must announce.

57. How much wealth, dear brothers and sisters, in the guidelines that the Second Vatican Council gave us! For this reason, in the preparation of the Great Jubilee, I have asked the Church to question itself about the reception of the Council[44]. Has it been done? The Congress that has been held here in the Vatican has been a moment of this reflection, and I hope that, in different ways, it has been carried out equally in all the particular Churches. As the years go by, those texts do not lose their value or their splendor. It is necessary to read them appropriately and for them to be known and assimilated as qualified and normative texts of the Magisterium, within the Tradition of the Church. After concluding the Jubilee I feel more than ever the duty to indicate the Council as the great grace from which the Church has benefited in the 20th century. With the Council we have been offered a sure compass to guide us on the path of the century that begins.

58. Let's walk with hope! A new millennium opens before the Church like an immense ocean in which we must venture, counting on the help of Christ. The Son of God, who was incarnated two thousand years ago for love of man, also carries out his work today. We must sharpen our eyes to see it and, above all, have a big heart to become its instruments. Was it not perhaps to make contact with this living spring of our hope that we celebrated the Jubilee Year? The contemplated and loved Christ now invites us once again to set out on the journey: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28,19). The missionary mandate introduces us to the third millennium, inviting us to have the same enthusiasm as the Christians of the early times. For this we can count on the strength of the same Spirit, who was sent at Pentecost and who pushes us to leave today, animated by the hope "that does not disappoint" (Rm 5,5).

59. Dear brothers and sisters! The symbol of the Holy Door closes behind our backs, but to leave the living door that is Christ open more than ever. After the jubilee enthusiasm we no longer return to a dull day to day. On the contrary, if our pilgrimage has been authentic, it should be like loosening our legs for the path that awaits us. We must imitate the fearlessness of the apostle Paul: “Lying forward toward what lies ahead, I run towards the goal, to obtain the prize to which God is calling me from on high, in Christ Jesus” (Flp 13,14). At the same time, we must imitate the contemplation of Mary, who, after the pilgrimage to the holy city of Jerusalem, returned to her home in Nazareth meditating in her heart the mystery of the Son (cf. Lc 2,51).
